A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BiScale-GTR study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and added material to be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original BiScale-GTR results on MoleculeNet, PharmaBench, and LRGB, alongside architecture ablations, tokenizer analyses, and attribution experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds tokenizer comparisons, vocabulary-size experiments, structural-attention ablations, masking analyses, and computational-cost measurements.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.1 changes the encoder description from GIN to GINE and replaces the neighbor sum in Equation 2 with ReLU(h_j + e_ij). However, v1 already states that edge embeddings enter message passing, and v2 still calls the encoder GIN in Section 4.2. The PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed or its description was corrected. The tokenizer, fusion, Transformer, and training objective otherwise remain consistent.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same approximately 430K ChEMBL molecules, seven MoleculeNet classification datasets, nine PharmaBench regression datasets, and Peptides-func/Peptides-struct. The added analyses use retained data and tasks rather than expanding dataset or domain coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds a substantial tokenizer comparison against atom tokenization, BRICS, and canonical-SMILES Graph-BPE in Table 5, plus a uniform-masking comparator in Table 21. These directly test central design choices beyond v1's comparisons. The main benchmark comparator sets and the earlier validity/OOV comparison remain present.

E3.justification: New protocols regenerate pretraining and downstream inputs for each tokenizer, vary target vocabulary sizes across 400/800/1600, retrain structural-bias ablations, and evaluate masked-fragment prediction accuracy and loss. Original splits, training budgets, and fine-tuning hyperparameters remain unchanged. The retained peptide tokenizer ablation also corrects its reported metric from ROC-AUC to AP, without establishing that it was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses testing alternative tokenizers, vocabulary size and chemical diversity, individual and combined attention biases, and frequency-aware versus uniform masking. It also examines pretraining reconstruction outcomes across masking ratios. The original GNN-depth study is retained as Appendix A.9/Table 19, rather than removed.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten seeds for main experiments and three runs for ablations, generally reporting means and standard deviations. The new three-run comparisons follow the existing replication scheme. No new confidence-interval, significance-testing, or uncertainty-estimation procedure is introduced; numerical discrepancies in reported deviations concern E6.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–3 retain their scores, but v2 adds substantial numerical evidence. For example, Table 5 reports MUV ROC-AUC of 81.6 for Graph-BPE + WL versus 73.0 for BRICS; Table 16 reports Peptides-func AP of 0.6571, 0.6717, and 0.6721 for target vocabularies of 400, 800, and 1600. New Table 18 also gives the full model's ToxCast result as 62.2 ± 0.9, inconsistent with 62.2 ± 0.2 in retained tables.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.4 supplies a complexity argument using bounded molecular degree and fixed WL rounds, reporting vocabulary-construction time O(KN n-bar) and inference-tokenization time O(n²), together with memory bounds. v2 also revises Equation 2 and formally defines visualization rank normalization. These are limited mathematical additions rather than a new theoretical foundation.

C1.justification: The central contribution is redefined from addressing GNN dominance and single-granularity modeling through a multiscale hybrid to grounding reusable fragment identities in occurrence-specific atomic context. v2 explicitly positions the architecture as serving this token-grounding problem rather than generic hybrid novelty. The abstract and contribution list also narrow the broad state-of-the-art assertion to strong benchmark performance.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of atom grounding, tokenizer advantages, vocabulary saturation, and structural-bias contributions. Appendix A.6.2 corrects the interpretation of Figure 7: vocabulary occurrence frequencies do not establish downstream token composition. It also explicitly qualifies fixed-vocabulary transfer, explains additional requirements for 3D extensions, and clarifies that Figure 3 colors express within-molecule ranks rather than biological effect sizes.

D1.justification: v1 promises code upon acceptance; v2 reports availability and supplies a repository link. New Appendix A.3 discloses vocabulary-construction, pretraining, fine-tuning, and inference costs, including eight GPU-hours for pretraining. Other additions specify bond-bias categories, tokenizer-control construction, fixed-sum fusion, and attribution normalization. These materially expand reproducibility information without proving that the underlying implementation changed.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially repositioned around reusable vocabularies, atom–fragment grounding, and fragment-level Transformers. New discussions include SPE, APE, GRAPHBPE, molecular-tokenization research, HiMol, HimGNN, and FragNet. The revised novelty argument distinguishes shared token identities from molecule-specific fragment representations, while several general GNN references are removed and attribution-supporting references are replaced.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting around shared fragment identities and atomic context. Related-work subsections are reorganized, experimental explanations are expanded, and the appendix is substantially restructured, including relocation of the GNN-depth discussion.

P2.justification: Seven tables are added for tokenizer comparisons, computational cost, vocabulary analyses, attention biases, and pretraining behavior. Figure 3 is recolored with explicit 0–1 rank-normalized scales and a revised caption. Existing tables are relocated or relabeled, including the GNN-depth table moving to the appendix; the other principal figures retain their underlying visual content.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for central design choices that v1 only partially tested, particularly through tokenizer alternatives, vocabulary-size sensitivity, attention-bias ablations, and the uniform-masking control. Clearer research positioning, more careful figure interpretation, and added code-access and runtime information further improve the paper. These gains outweigh the unresolved GIN/GINE description and isolated new reporting inconsistencies, including Table 18's ToxCast standard deviation. The improvement comes from stronger validation and documentation; headline benchmark scores are unchanged.
